intro: Martha Argerich plays a rhapsody that begins as a D♭-major march and ends with both hands flying through octaves in B♭ major. Between them come a quick dance and an ornamented slow song.

sections.label: A · March in D♭ major
sections.mNote: Steady bass chords support a melody that crosses the barlines

sections.label: B · Presto: the quick dance
sections.mNote: D♭ major is respelt C♯ major for the faster tune

sections.label: C · Andante: a B♭-minor song
sections.mNote: The piano sings slowly, with pauses and ornaments

sections.label: D · Allegro: the B♭-major dance
sections.mNote: A regular bass rhythm sets the tune dancing

sections.label: D′ · The tune in repeated octaves
sections.mNote: The right hand repeats each note with its octave

sections.label: Coda · Octaves in opposite directions
sections.mNote: Chromatic scales spread outwards towards the final B♭-major chords

relations.label: The quick dance repeats
relations.basis: The Presto dance is a repeated unit between the opening march and the Andante. Both excerpts fall within the 85–126 s Presto region rather than in the later octave variations. CENS diagonal mean 0.989, sustained 18.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 18.5 s (cache/form/liszt-hungarian-rhapsody-6.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: A march across the barlines
cues.text: The left hand sets down steady chords in D♭ major. Above them, the tune stretches across the barlines, tugging against the march’s two-beat tread. Liszt marks the opening Tempo giusto: a firm pulse, before the later flourishes take their liberties.
cues.evidence: The opening bass, metre and overlapping melody are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form. IMSLP confirms the opening marking and key: https://imslp.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No.6,_S.244/6_(Liszt,_Franz).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Songs in Liszt’s notebook
cues.text: Liszt writes down the tune of the short second section in 1840; three years later it appears in a folk-song collection. The opening melody also has a name, Chlopiczky.
cues.evidence: Leslie Howard identifies the first melody and dates Liszt’s notation of the second to 1840, before its 1843 publication: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA67418%2F9.

cues.title: Same keys, quicker feet
cues.text: After a flourish largely on the black keys, the Presto begins. D♭ major is now written as C♯ major: the same pitches with different names. The tune becomes a quick dance, with much less room between its steps.
cues.evidence: The cadenza, Presto heading and enharmonic change from D♭ to C♯ major are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A slow minor song
cues.text: The Andante turns to B♭ minor. The piano’s melody takes time over its ornaments and pauses, stretching each phrase after the quick dance. A long cadenza eventually carries the song towards the finale.
cues.evidence: The Andante in B♭ minor, its improvisatory rhythm and concluding cadenza are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Horváth’s song, printed in 1813
cues.text: The slow tune is by Ádám Pálóczi Horváth and appears in print in 1813. Liszt has already used it in his Rumanian Rhapsody before bringing it here.
cues.evidence: Leslie Howard identifies Horváth, the 1813 publication and Liszt’s earlier use in the Rumanian Rhapsody: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA67418%2F9.

cues.title: B♭ turns to major
cues.text: The Allegro keeps B♭ and changes minor to major. A repeated quaver rhythm in the bass supports the quick tune above it. This is the friss, the fast dance that will occupy the rest of the rhapsody.
cues.evidence: The Allegro in B♭ major and repeated quaver bass are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The right hand doubles up
cues.text: The tune is doubled in octaves and hammered out in quick repetitions. Each melodic note sounds at two pitches, an octave apart, while the left hand keeps the dance rhythm beneath it. A melody has become an endurance test for one hand.
cues.evidence: The finale’s semiquaver octave melody and repeated quaver accompaniment are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The hands pull apart
cues.text: Chromatic scales in octaves send the hands in opposite directions. The closing chords land in B♭ major, the finale’s key; the opening march’s D♭ major is a long way behind.
cues.evidence: The contrary-motion chromatic octaves and closing B♭-major chords are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Black-key flourish, then Presto
transitions.how: A piano cadenza, largely on the black keys, separates the march from the Presto. Liszt respells D♭ major as C♯ major, keeping the same tonic pitch. The measured bass chords of the opening make way for the quick dance.
transitions.evidence: The opening cadenza and the Presto’s C♯-major notation are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form.

transitions.title: From quick dance to slow song
transitions.how: The Presto closes, and the Andante begins in B♭ minor, the relative minor of the opening D♭ major. The piano abandons the quick dance rhythm for a melody with pauses and ornaments. Its phrases now have room to sound like improvised singing.
transitions.evidence: The succession of Presto and Andante, their keys and the slow section’s improvisatory rhythm are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form.

transitions.title: The cadenza releases B♭ major
transitions.how: The Andante ends with a long piano cadenza. The following Allegro turns B♭ minor into B♭ major, replacing D♭ with D♮. Repeated quavers in the bass give the fast tune a regular dancing step.
transitions.evidence: The slow section’s final cadenza and the Allegro’s B♭-major key and repeated bass rhythm are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form.

transitions.title: One tune, doubled in octaves
transitions.to: D′ · The tune in repeated octaves
transitions.how: In the B♭-major finale, Liszt doubles the tune in octaves and repeats its notes in semiquavers. The left hand maintains the quaver rhythm beneath it. The melody continues through the right hand’s rapid jumps.
transitions.evidence: The finale’s octave melody and quaver bass are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form.

transitions.title: Octaves pull the hands apart
transitions.from: D′ · The tune in repeated octaves
transitions.how: The closing piano runs turn into chromatic scales in octaves, the hands moving in opposite directions. These lead to the final B♭-major chords. The dance’s key holds to the end.
transitions.evidence: The contrary-motion chromatic octave scales and B♭-major conclusion are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._6, under Form.

composer.born: 22 October 1811, Doborján, Kingdom of Hungary (now Raiding, Austria)
composer.epithet: He could fit an orchestra under ten fingers, then end a lifetime at the piano with a few notes left hanging in the air.
facts: Carl Czerny and Antonio Salieri in Vienna; Anton Reicha in Paris
Free masterclasses; founding president of the Budapest music academy, 1875
Piano works and transcriptions; thirteen symphonic poems; symphonies, concertos and sacred music
composer.background:
Writing from Albano in June 1839, Liszt told Princess Cristina Belgiojoso about the concerts he had been giving alone in Rome. No singer came on between his pieces; no other soloist shared the bill. He played his transcription of the William Tell Overture, fantasies on opera tunes, studies and improvisations. Between numbers he talked to the audience. “The concert is me,” he joked. A single pianist had taken possession of an entire evening.

His father Adam had begun the piano lessons in Doborján, a German-speaking village in the Kingdom of Hungary, where he worked on an Esterházy estate. Hungary remained Liszt’s homeland, though German and French were the languages he used most easily. The family went to Vienna in 1822. Carl Czerny, a former pupil of Beethoven, taught him piano; Antonio Salieri taught him composition. Paris followed in 1823, but its Conservatoire refused to admit a foreigner. Private lessons, including work with Anton Reicha, continued his education.
